where the integrator is discretized using backward Euler discretization with sampling period \(T_{s}\). \(\gamma\) is the integral gain. In fact, \(C\) shows a generalized PID structure, where the proportional and derivative terms are replaced by a FIR filter.

\(C\) can be easily designed from data, following the approach of virtual reference feedback tuning [10]. In Figure 1, we represent the desired closed-loop performance with a time-invariant (possibly nonlinear) reference model \(M_{r}\). \(P\) is a time-invariant single-input single-output plant. The plant is not necessarily linear but we assume _passivity_ from the input \(u\) to the output \(y\) (e.g. Euler-Lagrangian systems and port-Hamiltonian systems [1], [19]). For any given reference \(r\), the ideal closed-loop behavior satisfies \(y \simeq y^{*}\).

**Fig. 1.** Block diagram of the closed-loop system.

The controller can be derived as the solution of the following optimization problem:

\[\min_{C \in \text{IFIR}} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{t=0}^{N-1} \left( u(t) - C(M_{r}^{-1}(y) - y)(t) \right)^{2}
\tag{2}\]

where \(\{ y(t) \}_{t=0,\ldots,N-1}\) is the measured open-loop plant output when the plant is excited with a user-defined signal \(\{ u(t) \}_{t=0,\ldots,N-1}\). The output signal \(y\) can be obtained by experiments, making the approach suitable for settings where a plant model is not fully available.

Under the ideal condition of perfect matching \(y = y^{*}\), the idea of VRFT is to derive a compatible reference signal \(r = M_{r}^{-1}y^{*} = M_{r}^{-1}y\), which is then used to obtain the controller \(C\) by fitting the input/output pair \((r - y, u)\). The inverse reference model \(M_{r}^{-1}\) is realized by a causal approximation. For linear reference models, the inverse can be removed by filtering of input and output signals via \(M_{r}\) itself, which leads to the filtered optimization problem

\[\min_{C \in \text{IFIR}} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{t=0}^{N-1} \left( M_{r} u(t) - C(y - M_{r}y)(t) \right)^{2}
\tag{3}\]

Following [10], for linear plants and linear reference models, the minimizer of (2) also minimizes

\[\min_{C(z)} \left\| M_{r}(z) - \frac{P(z)C(z)}{1 + P(z)C(z)} \right\|_{2}^{2}
\tag{4}\]

if the optimal controller of the latter, \(C^{*}(z)\), can be represented by an iFIR (1) (for \(N \to \infty\) and if \(u\) is given by the realization of a stationary and ergodic stochastic process). If \(C^{*} \notin \text{iFIR}\), pre-filtering of the open-loop data \(\{ u(t), y(t) \}_{t=0,\ldots,N-1}\) with a suitably chosen LTI filter can reduce the difference between the two minimizers. We refer to [10] for additional details on VRFT.

The optimization problems in (2) and (3) are equivalent to a least-squares problem and hence can be solved efficiently.


For instance, take \(e = M_{r}^{-1}(y) - y\). From [20, Eq. 7.3], the optimization problem (2) (or (3)) with the controller (1) reads

\[\min_{g \in \mathbb{R}^{m}} \left\| u - Eg - \gamma E_{\text{int}} \right\|_{2}^{2}
\tag{5}\]

where \(g = [g_{0} \ldots g_{m-1}]^{T}\), \(u = [u(0) \ldots u(N-1)]^{T}\),

\[E = 
\begin{bmatrix}
e(0) & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 
e(1) & e(0) & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & 0 \\ 
e(N-2) & e(N-3) & \cdots & e(N-m) & 1 \\ 
e(N-1) & e(N-2) & \cdots & e(N-m)
\end{bmatrix},\]

and \(E_{\text{int}} = T_{s}\left[ e(0) & e(0)+e(1) & \cdots & \sum_{t=1}^{N-1} e(t) \right]^{T}\). If the input is persistently exciting, then \(E\) will be full rank and a unique solution exists [4, Section 3.2]. In what follows, in our extension of VRFT based on passive iFIR controller, uniqueness of solution is not necessary to guarantee closed-loop stability. Therefore, this rank condition will not be considered again.

**III. PASSIVE iFIR CONTROLLERS**

Although VRFT is an established and effective design methodology, the data-driven optimal controller (2) _does not guarantee closed-loop stability_. For passive plants \(P\), we tackle this issue through passivity. We combine the least-square fitting (5) with specific constraints that enforce passivity. This leads to the derivation of the passive iFIR controller that best fits the desired input / output data (2).

The first formulation is a straightforward application of the Kalman-Yakubovich-Popov (KYP) lemma.

**Theorem 3.1 (KYP approach):** Given the iFIR (1) of order \(m\), consider the state-space realization of the FIR part

\[\begin{cases}
x(t+1) = A_{c}x(t) + B_{e}w(t) \\
z(t) = C_{c}x(t) + D_{e}w(t)
\end{cases}
\tag{6}\]

where \(w(t), z(t)\) are the input and output of the FIR part. \(A_{c} \in \mathbb{R}^{m-1 \times m-1}, B_{c} \in \mathbb{R}^{m-1}, C_{c} \in \mathbb{R}^{m-1}, D_{c} \in \mathbb{R}\) are given by

\[A_{c} = 
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 
0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & 0 \\ 
0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 \\ 
0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}, \quad B_{c} = 
\begin{bmatrix}
0 \\ 
0 \\ 
\vdots \\ 
0 \\ 
1
\end{bmatrix}\]

\[C_{c} = 
\begin{bmatrix}
g_{m-1} & g_{m-2} & \cdots & g_{2} & g_{1}
\end{bmatrix}, \quad D_{c} = g_{0}.\]

The optimal iFIR controller given by (2) constrained to the following LMIs in the unknown \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{m-1 \times m-1}\), \(C_{c}\), and \(D_{c}\)

\[\gamma \geq 0 \quad (7a)\]

\[X = X^{T} > 0 \quad (7b)\]

\[\begin{bmatrix}
X - A_{c}^{T}X \\
C_{c} - B_{c}^{T}X
\end{bmatrix}C_{c} - A_{c}^{T}X B_{c} \geq 0 \quad (7c)\]

\[D_{c} + D_{c}^{T} \geq 0 \quad (7d)\]

is passive, thus guarantees closed-loop stability.

安全的。Compared with the KYP approach of Theorem 3.1, the finite Toeplitz approach of Theorem 3.2 leads to an optimization problem with \(o(m)\) unknowns, linear in the order \(m\) of the iFIR filter. However, for a fixed \(\epsilon\) (or \(n\)), the value of \(n\) (or \(\epsilon\)) that leads to passivity is bounded by some finite but unknown \(n^*\) (by some finite \(\epsilon^*\)), thus needs to be tuned iteratively. The following theorem overcomes this limitation. Given the coefficients \(g = g_k\), in what follows we use \(G(e^{j\theta})\) to denote its frequency response \(\sum_{k=0}^{m-1} g_k e^{-jk\theta}\).

**Theorem 3.4 (Positive realness approach):** Given the iFIR (1) of order \(m\), let \(g = \{g_k\}_{k=0,\ldots,m-1}\) be the finite coefficients of its FIR part. For any \(\rho_0 > 0, 0 < \rho \leq 1, M \geq 2\) the iFIR controller by (2) and

\[
\begin{align*}
\gamma \geq 0 \tag{14a} \\
\rho_0 \geq |g_0| \tag{14b} \\
\rho_0 \rho^k \geq |g_k| \quad \forall k \in \{1, \ldots, m-1\} \tag{14c}
\end{align*}
\]

\[
G(e^{j\theta}) + G(e^{-j\theta}) \geq \epsilon \quad \forall q \in \{0, \ldots, M\} \tag{14d} \\
\epsilon = \pi \rho_0 \frac{1 - \rho^m}{1 - \rho} \frac{m-1}{2M} \tag{14e}
\]

is passive.

**Proof:** We focus on the FIR part of the filter, to show that (14) implies positive realness, i.e. \(G(e^{j\theta}) + G(e^{-j\theta}) \geq 0\) for all \(\theta\). The latter is equivalent to

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{m-1} g_k \cos(k\theta) \geq 0 \quad \forall \theta \in [0, \pi]. \tag{15}
\]

As first step, we need the following bound. Take \(f(\theta) = \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} g_k \cos(k\theta)\). For all \(\theta\) and \(\Delta\), we have

\[
|f(\theta + \Delta) - f(\theta)| \leq \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} |g_k| |\cos(k\theta + k\Delta) - \cos(k\theta)| \\
\leq \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} |g_k| |k\Delta| \\
\leq (m-1)|\Delta| \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} |g_k|. \tag{16}
\]

We now use (14). Let us sample \(f\) at \(M+1\) points over the domain \([0, \pi]\) with a sampling interval \(\frac{1}{M}\). That is, consider \(f(g_{\theta}, \theta)\) for \(q \in \{0, \ldots, M\}\). Then, for any given \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\), find the closest sample point \(\frac{q}{M}\pi\) to \(\theta\) and take \(\Delta = \theta - \frac{q}{M}\pi\). By construction, \(-\frac{\pi}{2M} \leq \Delta \leq \frac{\pi}{2M}\) and (16) guarantees that

\[
|f(\theta) - f(g_{\pi\over M})| = |f(g_{\pi\over M} + \Delta) - f(g_{\pi\over M})| \\
\leq (m-1)|\Delta| \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} |g_k| \\
\leq m - 1 \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} |g_k|\]
where the last inequality follows from (14b) and (14c), since \(g_k = g_{\theta + \frac{1}{M}\pi}\).

Thus, from (17), it is easy to see that (14d) and (14e) guarantee \(G(e^{j\theta}) + G(e^{-j\theta}) = f(\theta) \geq 0\).

Theorem 3.4 follows closely [17, Section III.B] and [18, Section 2] but guarantees passivity with a finite length of training data and a finite number of constraints in the context of data-driven control design. Compared with Theorem 3.3, Theorem 3.4 leads to a one-shot design approach. The theorem illustrates that passivity can be enforced by constraining the sampled frequency response of the FIR to be larger than a certain constant \(\epsilon\), which depends on the decay rate of the impulse response, the order of the FIR part, and the number of sampling points in the frequency domain. This is equivalent to verifying that the sampled Nyquist diagram of the FIR subcontroller has a real part greater than \(\epsilon\). In this case, \(\epsilon\) bounds the maximal variation of the real part of the Nyquist diagram between each two samples.

From the proof of Theorem 3.4, it can be seen that the bound (14e) on \(\epsilon\) is conservative. Conservativeness is reduced by increasing the number of samples \(M\), that is, by enforcing a larger number of constraints. The trade-off between the computational complexity and conservativeness can be mitigated by replacing the bound (14e) with an heuristic search over \(\epsilon\), based on an iteration similar to the one derived from Theorem 3.3. In terms of complexity, Theorem 3.4 is more efficient than Theorems 3.1 and 3.3 since there are no LMIs involved. Furthermore, (14d) can be implemented with \(M+1\) linear inequality constraints of the form (15), for \(\theta = \frac{q\pi}{M}\) and \(q \in \{0, \ldots, M\}\).

**Remark 3.5:** The constrained optimization (2) subject to passivity constraints is always feasible. For instance, for any \(\epsilon^* \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(\gamma \geq 0\), consider the iFIR controller in (1) given by \(g_0 \geq \epsilon^*\) and \(g_k = 0, \forall k > 0\). If \(\epsilon^* \geq 0\), this iFIR controller is compatible with (7). If \(\epsilon^*\) is larger than the \(\epsilon\) chosen in (10) or (14e), then this iFIR controller is compatible with (10) or (14), respectively.

**Remark 3.6:** The phase correction that a passive linear controller can introduce is limited to \(\pm 90\) degrees. This poses a limit on the achievable performance. The level of conservativeness depends on the performance requirement, based on the selected reference model \(M_r\).

### IV. EXAMPLES

#### A. Fitting of passive FIR filters

We identify passive FIR filters to illustrate the effectiveness of (7), (10) and (14) in dealing with the targets

\[c_q(s) = \frac{1}{(0.5s + 1)^q} \quad q \in \{1, 2, 3\}, \tag{18}\]

where \(C_1\) is passive, and \(C_2\) and \(C_3\) show increase shortage of passivity. For each target, we take \(\gamma = 0\) and (5) paired with passivity constraints. The input/output data \((e, u)\) are generated as \(u = C_ie\) for \(i \in \{1, 2, 3\}\). The probing signal is a filtered step given by \(e = \mathcal{L}^{-1} \left(\frac{1}{0.2s + 1}\frac{1}{s}\right)\), where \(\mathcal{L}^{-1}\) is the inverse Laplace transform. Results are shown in Figure 2. The top-left plot shows that all three approaches give perfect fitting. The top-right plot shows the results for conservative \(\epsilon\) (10d). B. Velocity control of a compliant mechanical system
Consider the two-cart plant of Figure 3, modeling a truck pulling a heavy load. The cart masses are \(m_{1} = 3.0\) kg, \(m_{2} = 0.5\) kg. \(k_{12} = 1.0\) Ns/m is the spring stiffness and \(c_{12} = 1.05\) Ns/m is the damping coefficient. Each cart is also affected by additional dissipation of the form \(c\dot{x}_{i}\), where \(c = 0.5\) Ns/m and \(\dot{x}_{i}\) is the absolute velocity of the cart \(i \in \{1, 2\}\). The block diagram for this closed-loop system is represented in Figure 1. \(u\) is the applied force and \(y\) is the velocity output.

where \(\zeta = 1\), \(T_{1} = 0.25\)s, \(T_{2} = 0.125\)s. \(M_{r2}\) is more aggressive because it has a higher cutoff frequency.
